preamble: Raising of the open-mid front vowel [ɛ] to close-mid [e], often as one step in a chain shift or as a merger of the two front mid vowels. Attic η /ɛː/ rose to /eː/ in early Koine, Middle English /ɛː/ (meat) rose to /eː/ in the second phase of the Great Vowel Shift, and in contemporary South Korean the vowels ㅐ /ɛ/ and ㅔ /e/ have merged as [e̞].

examples.note: After /eː/ (spelled ει) rose to /iː/ in the late 4th–3rd centuries BC, the open-mid long vowels /ɛː ɔː/ shifted to close-mid /eː oː/; η later went on to /i/.
In the second phase of the Great Vowel Shift the open-mid long vowels /ɛː ɔː/ raised to /eː oː/; meat later merged with meet in /iː/.
In South Korean speech the /ɛ/–/e/ contrast is lost and both are most commonly realized as [e̞]; some older speakers keep the distinction.
Pre-Hlai and Proto-Hlai forms are Norquest's (2015) reconstructions as listed in the Wiktionary appendix; Peripheral Vowel Raising raised long *ɛː to *eː, alongside *e > *i and *o > *u before codas.
